extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and documenting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including treatment of prior art, analogous-art analysis, applicant traverses and rebuttal evidence. Intended to direct examiner practice and inform applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant traverse requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. An effective traverse must not be merely a conclusory assertion; it must 'distinctly and specifically' identify errors. If insufficient, Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective traverse when disputing Office factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement or argument that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence is not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Applicants should supply specific, reasoned explanations; otherwise the examiner may reiterate the rejection and proceed to finality (MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Examiners must reconsider initial obviousness determinations in view of the entire record and articulate findings of fact supporting their rationale. Review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability; follow procedures in MPEP §706.07(a) when determining finality. See MPEP §2145 and §716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 for traversing grounds of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of rebuttal evidence for combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of evidence or argument applicants may submit to rebut a combination-based obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may demonstrate that (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Such evidence should be timely presented and considered in conjunction with the entire record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art availability under 35 U.S.C. 102 for use in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art may be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of whether it otherwise qualifies under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102. See case law (Panduit; Ex parte Andresen) and MPEP §§901, 2121-2129, 2151-2155 for overview and details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections and specific 35 U.S.C. 102 categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), 102(b), 102(e), etc., depending on the type of prior art reference used and its publication or issue date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, an obviousness rejection over a U.S. patent issued more than one year before filing may be treated as a statutory bar under pre-AIA 102(b). A rejection based on a publication that could be applied under pre-AIA 102(a) may be overcome by swearing behind the publication via 37 CFR 1.131. Examiners should identify the applicable 102 basis when making a 103 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of the prior art (enabling, inoperative devices, admissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation of prior art for obviousness includes consideration of the substantive content of the prior art: availability of inoperative devices, extent to which prior art must be enabling, whether a disclosure is broad or limited to preferred embodiments, admissions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2121-§2129 for relevant case law. Examiners must analyze what the prior art actually teaches or suggests, and whether it would enable a person of ordinary skill to practice the relevant aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal perspective to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art must be determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers should 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made' and consider what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at that time. See W.L. Gore v. Garlock and MPEP §2145 for discussion of rebutting hindsight arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden to show applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to invoke pre-AIA 103(c) has the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research agreement benefits the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §2146.01 and §2146.02 and related case law for limits and date-related restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for use in an obviousness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). Examiners must determine analogous art for obviousness analysis and cite supporting reasons and case law (In re Bigio; KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proof of 'reasonably pertinent' art
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reasonably pertinent' art must 'logically [] have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining reasonable pertinence, consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification. To support a determination that a reference is reasonably pertinent, it may be appropriate to include an examiner's statement of understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent. The perception of the problem can affect the scope of available prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner consideration of applicant's argument on nonanalogous art
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument by the applicant that the examiner has misconstrued the problem to be solved, and thereby improperly relied on nonanalogous art, should be fully considered in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the applicant's argument by looking to the teachings of the specification and inferences reasonably drawn by a person of ordinary skill. If the applicant persuasively shows the problem was misconceived, the examiner should reassess whether the reference qualifies as analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of structural and functional similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry far greater weight than mere classification when assessing analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Patent Office classification and cross-references provide evidence, courts give greater weight to structural/functional comparison. Examiners should analyze structural and functional overlap when deciding whether a reference is analogous (In re Ellis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous-art application across specific arts (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous-art principles apply across different technological arts; examples illustrate how courts applied the tests in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use art-specific factual analysis: e.g., in chemical arts consider whether teachings in one chemistry area would be pertinent to another; in mechanical arts consider similar problems across device types; in electrical arts consider problem similarity like rate-limiting; in design arts consider general use. Case citations provide precedential examples (Ex parte Bland; Stratoflex; Bigio; Medtronic; In re Rosen, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret claim language and consider invention and references as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences between prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§2111-2116.01 for claim interpretation law. Consider whether claim language limits the scope and how limitations weight in the overall obviousness analysis (MPEP §2143.03 for claim-limiting examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole' in obviousness inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on a single difference or element; evaluate the combination and overall invention (Stratoflex; Schenck; In re Hirao). Admissions of unobviousness for some elements can render the combination nonobvious when considered as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distilling the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show that focusing on a single advantage or treating claims as though they read differently than allowed is improper. Examiners should not ignore express claim limitations or reduce the claimed invention to a one-word solution or a single concept (W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb; Panduit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of source/ cause of a problem considered in 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the source or cause of a problem may be part of the patentable subject matter when analyzing the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While identifying the source of a problem can support patentability (In re Sponnoble), it does not always yield a patentable invention if the solution was obvious from prior art that contained the same solution (In re Wiseman). Examiners should assess whether the prior art would have suggested the same solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery of a problem source must substantiate
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who allege the inventor discovered the source of a problem must provide evidence substantiating the allegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence can be affidavits/declarations or a clear and persuasive assertion in the specification. Unsubstantiated counsel statements are insufficient (In re Wiseman; In re Kaslow). Examiners should require substantive support when such claims are presented.
